title: Who killed Billy Hall? Retired lawyer probes 1967 murder of Cape Breton teen
summary: William (Billy) Hall was just 16 when he moved from North Sydney, N.S., to Ontario in late 1966 seeking better economic opportunities, as many of his siblings had before him. Within less than a year,…

image.caption: William (Billy) Hall was quiet and kind, had brown hair and freckles, and loved bowling. (Ontario Provincial Police)

blocks.text: William (Billy) Hall was just 16 when he moved from North Sydney, N.S., to Ontario in late 1966 for better opportunities, as many of his 12 siblings had before him.

Less than a year later, the quiet and kind teen with brown hair and freckles who loved bowling was murdered. Hall had set out in search of work on a tobacco farm, only to be found with a gunshot wound to the back of his head and one hand missing.

The case remains unsolved, and a retired Ontario lawyer has become obsessed with it — scouring newspaper archives, tracking down historical photos and filing freedom-of-information requests in hopes of finding a lead that breaks the case.
"I am motivated by the fact that someone did a very heinous thing to another human being and got away with it," said Jason Ward.

"Whether that's one person or more and whether they're dead or alive, I do feel a really strong sense that justice needs to be served ... The other side of it is that, you know, I won't call it [obsessive-compulsive disorder], but it's that wiring inside of me that compels me to do this, this challenge that once it gets inside me, I have a very difficult time managing it."
Jason Ward, a retired lawyer, has launched a website with information about Hall's murder and is pushing authorities to be more transparent about their work on the case. (Submitted by Jason Ward)
While Ward owns a law practice, he no longer practises and now speaks publicly about mental health and addiction, the latter of which nearly derailed his legal career.
Ward has also launched a website and social media campaign posing the question: Who killed Billy Hall?
A sister's appeal
For Marie McGean, it's a question that's lingered for almost six decades. She's the youngest of the 13 Hall children, of whom seven are still alive.
"There's somebody out there that knows something," she said. "There's always somebody out there that knows somebody that knows something."
McGean was 12 when she last saw Billy, bidding him goodbye at the North Sydney train station in November 1966. When he boarded, his seat was on the opposite side from the platform.
"That always bothered me ... I couldn't wave to him as the train was pulling out," said McGean.
Billy Hall's life in July 1967
In July 1967, Hall was living in Port Credit, Ont. It's now part of Mississauga, about 30 kilometres southwest of Toronto.
He worked at Hollywood Kitchen, doing odd jobs in the back shop, according to the Aug. 8, 1967, edition of The Weekly.
A company employee, Mrs. Robert Cushnaghan, told the newspaper that Hall was a good worker who did what he was told. She said they were sorry to see him go.
"I tried to talk him out of it, to convince him to stay, but he said he had to go and make something of his life," Cushnaghan told the newspaper.
Hall's 1956 Chevrolet Bel Air is shown. (www.whokilledbillyhall.ca)

When Hall left Port Credit on July 19, 1967, he was four days shy of 17. He told family members he planned to travel with someone to look for work on a tobacco farm in Bowmanville, Ont., but he didn't name the person.
Bowmanville is about 100 kilometres northeast of Port Credit.
On July 31, 1967, Hall's body was found in dense bush about 15 metres from a roadway near Pontypool, roughly 24 kilometres north of Bowmanville, the Aug. 2, 1967, Toronto Telegram reported.
Police suspected Hall was shot elsewhere and his body dumped at the scene up to two weeks earlier, given the state of decomposition.

Hall's family didn't know he was dead until after his burial. Assuming he was working on a tobacco farm, they had not reported him missing. The body was identified only after a relative spotted a matching description in the newspaper.
This article on the Hall case appeared in the Toronto Star of Aug. 2, 1967. (www.newspapers.com)

On Aug. 3, 1967, after identifying Hall's clothing, two relatives travelling with an Ontario Provincial Police inspector spotted his car — with a flat tire — at a Toronto construction site near Highway 401 and the Don Valley Parkway.
The Toronto Telegram called discovering the car a "million-to-one chance."
Department of Highways records showed the vehicle had been there since July 22 — three days after Hall was last seen — according to a 2016 article in the Kawartha Lakes This Week.
Hall's vehicle was a black 1956 Chevrolet Bel Air. Newspaper accounts say he purchased it, but McGean said it was given to him by one of his brothers.
Ward said no one knows how the car ended up at the construction site, though some have speculated Hall hitchhiked after it broke down.
Part of an Aug. 16, 1967, article from The Weekly, a Port Credit-area, Ont., newspaper, is shown. (Submitted by Jason Ward)
A $2,000 reward for information to help solve the case was offered in late August 1967.
At 12, and as one of only two of Hall's 13 siblings still living in North Sydney, McGean felt distanced from the ordeal.

"I felt that separation part from it and I felt really bad for the ones that were there [in Ontario] that were older because I know they would feel guilty, you know, feel responsible and everything," said McGean.
Initial media coverage was extensive before quickly fizzling out, though a line from an Oct. 7, 1967, Oshawa Times article proved prescient.

An OPP spokesperson told the newspaper that it was unusual for a case to drag on this long without new evidence. Without a breakthrough, the spokesperson said "it could still be open 50 years from now."
Project Millennium

In 2015, Hall's murder was assigned to an Ontario Provincial Police investigator as part of Project Millennium, which examines historical unsolved homicides, the Kawaratha Lakes This Week reported. A year later, the reward was upped to $50,000.

In Kawartha Lakes This Week's 2016 reporting, a new detail emerged about the case. It reported a witness told police they drove a young man to Bowmanville and gave him the names of two tobacco farms. The hitchhiker also mentioned owning a car matching Hall's 1956 Chevrolet Bel Air.
DNA may offer the best hope for a breakthrough. In 2017, the paper reported that DNA and fingerprints had been extracted from crime-scene evidence.
Whether genetic genealogy has been used in the investigation is unclear.
"I think that's probably the best prospect of solving the case," said Ward.
Status of police investigation
OPP declined an interview request, saying in a statement that its historical homicide unit continues to investigate using modern investigative methods and forensic technology.
It said it could not comment "on specific investigative techniques or provide details regarding the ongoing review," but encouraged anyone with information to come forward.
Marie McGean of North Sydney, N.S., says knowing her brother was first buried in Ontario in 1967 without his family present makes her sad. (Submitted by Marie McGean)
McGean said the gap between when Hall was last seen and when his body was found, along with his quiet nature and small circle of friends, made generating leads difficult.
She said the OPP detective assigned during Project Millennium communicated frequently with the family, but since his retirement, the case has hit a standstill.

Ward agrees the investigation has stalled. He said his freedom-of-information requests for investigative records and coroner's reports were denied, prompting him to appeal to the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario.
Hall's headstone at Holy Cross Cemetery in North Sydney, N.S., is shown. He was initially buried in Ontario, but his remains were later transferred to Nova Scotia. (Submitted by Marie McGean)
McGean remembers Billy working a part-time job to scrape together enough money to buy her and another brother second-hand bikes.
"To us, it was like, 'Wow!' Yeah, we didn't have much," she said.
But the lack of answers still weighs on her, especially for the brothers Hall lived with in Ontario — first David, and then Larry, who died in 2019.
"I did feel like I failed my family and especially my brother Larry," McGean wrote in an email. "He was someone with a heart of gold. He was everyone's go-to guy."
How Ward learned about the case

Ward first heard about the case in passing about a decade ago, but has immersed himself in it only over the last five months, spending roughly $2,500 out of pocket. He's also trying to find partnerships to pay for billboard advertisements and DNA testing.
Asked if he's generated any promising leads through his investigation, Ward said yes, but declined to detail them on the grounds it could compromise the police investigation.

"My ultimate goal is to identify the killer, alive or dead, and if alive, for that killer to be prosecuted," said Ward. "And if that killer is dead, then to make it publicly known what that person did while living because I think the honour of Billy and his family depend on that."
